value.overview: The Ochre-breasted Antpitta (Grallaricula flavirostris) is a small, secretive forest bird of the antpitta family. It spends most of its time on or near the ground in dense, humid mountain forest, where it searches among leaf litter and low vegetation for small invertebrates. Its rounded body, short tail, yellowish bill, and warm ochre breast are distinctive, but its skulking habits make it easier to hear than see. It ranges from Costa Rica through Panama and the Andes to Bolivia.
value.classification: The Ochre-breasted Antpitta belongs to the family Grallariidae in the order Passeriformes. Several geographic subspecies are recognized, including the Costa Rican form, Grallaricula flavirostris costaricensis.
value.identification: This is a small, compact antpitta with olive-brown to brown upperparts, a short tail, rounded wings, and a relatively stout yellowish bill. The underparts are warm ochre or buff, with the breast typically richer and more orange than the belly. Fine markings can vary among subspecies. It usually keeps its body low, moves by short hops, and disappears quickly into thick vegetation. In Costa Rica, its clear, repeated whistle is often the best way to detect it.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Costa Rica and western Panama south through the Andes of Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, the resident subspecies costaricensis is found mainly in humid montane and cloud forests, especially on the Caribbean slope from central Alajuela southward, with additional local populations on the Pacific slope from central San José southward. It favors mature, shaded forest with dense understory, moss, leaf litter, and relatively undisturbed ground cover, generally at middle to upper elevations.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a resident species rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, it is present year-round in suitable montane forest, although local movements may occur with changes in food availability or conditions.
value.breeding: The breeding biology of the Ochre-breasted Antpitta is not fully documented. Nests have been described in Costa Rica and are placed low in dense vegetation, where they are concealed near the forest floor. The nest is a small cup made from plant material, and both adults are believed to participate in territorial defense and parental care. Breeding activity has been recorded during the wet season in parts of its range, but timing may vary geographically.
value.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly on small invertebrates, including insects, spiders, and other arthropods. The bird forages alone or in pairs on the forest floor, pausing frequently before hopping forward and probing leaf litter, loose soil, moss, and low vegetation. It may make short pounces to capture prey and generally remains under dense cover rather than feeding in exposed places.
value.behavior: The Ochre-breasted Antpitta is shy, quiet, and strongly terrestrial. It usually moves slowly through shadowy understory and leaf litter, often freezing when disturbed and then slipping away without flying far. Its short wings and reduced tail reflect its ground-oriented lifestyle. Individuals defend territories with clear, repeated whistles, and pairs may respond to one another from dense vegetation. Sightings are uncommon because the species is more often heard than observed.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend has not been quantified reliably.
